script.text: Serbia's longtime leader conceded defeat to a student movement. Israel woke up without a majority. And Iran's foreign minister says a plan to reopen a route for a fifth of the world's oil, in two days, is under discussion.

Five stories, ranked by impact. Number one is the diplomacy that may decide whether the Iran war moves toward talks or toward new strikes, with the key dates only days away. And one number from Europe is what Germany's chancellor says that war has cost.

Number five is a vote in Serbia. On Sunday, October twenty-fifth, Serbians voted in a snap parliamentary election. Preliminary results from the electoral commission gave the Student List about fifty-three percent of the vote and one hundred forty of the two hundred fifty seats. That is an outright majority. The ruling list of President Aleksandar Vucic won about thirty-nine percent and one hundred four seats. Vucic conceded in a short statement. He said the students had won and would hold between one hundred thirty-five and one hundred forty seats, while his side would have around one hundred five. Al Jazeera reported the highest turnout in decades. The movement began after a railway station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad in November twenty twenty-four, killing sixteen people, according to most reports. Students then led protests for almost two years. NPR reported that most established opposition parties stepped aside rather than run against the students. These results are preliminary, and the Student List has no single leader, so who becomes prime minister is still open. The European Policy Centre, a Brussels think tank, calls the result a test for the European Union.

Number four is Israel, a country that voted and still has no government. Final results published Friday by the Central Elections Committee, reported by the Times of Israel and NBC News, give Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc fifty-three seats. The bloc behind his challenger, former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, has forty-eight. Arab-led parties won nineteen. The Knesset has one hundred twenty seats, and a majority takes sixty-one. Neither side gets there alone. Netanyahu's Likud is the largest single party, with twenty-seven seats. Turnout was seventy-seven point nine percent. Eisenkot has said he will not serve in a government led by Netanyahu, including in a rotation. CNBC reports that Netanyahu's party claims the election was stolen, while the Central Elections Committee said an investigation into alleged voter fraud will not affect the final results. Next, President Isaac Herzog consults the parties and names someone to try to build a coalition. According to reports, that can take twenty-eight days, plus up to fourteen more. If it fails, Israel could face yet another election. Iran and Gaza were among the main issues in the campaign, according to pre-election coverage by CNN and NPR.

Number three is a bill. On October thirtieth, in South Korea, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said, according to reports, that the conflict around Iran has cost Europe a huge sum in higher energy prices over about eight months. Quick question: how much, according to Merz? Take a guess. More than one hundred billion euros. Merz did not explain how he calculated it, and he said the conflict cannot be solved militarily. No breakdown by country or industry was given. According to reports, Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, answered sharply. He said one hundred billion euros is nothing compared with the earth-shattering blow that Iran's armed forces would deal to anyone who harms its people. Oil is still expensive. According to Investing dot com, Brent crude closed Friday at about one hundred thirteen dollars a barrel, up about one and a half percent on the week. Fuel, heating and many everyday goods depend on energy prices. In March, at the start of the war, Euronews reported that European gas prices had jumped about sixty percent.

Number two is a countdown to November third. On October twenty-eighth, the Wall Street Journal reported that the United States told several Gulf Arab states to prepare for a possible short, intense military campaign against Iran after the midterm elections. One outlet, Roya News, named a date: November fourth, the day after the vote. The other reports named none. Fox News reported that an additional aircraft carrier strike group and a Marine expeditionary unit are being repositioned toward the region, and that a Patriot missile system is going to Israel. Asked about strikes after the midterms, President Trump said anything is possible. He has also said he will not attack before the vote. News reports say no final decision has been made, and that the preparations are not a green light. On Saturday, October thirty-first, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump has made no choice yet on resuming military action. Gulf states are pushing for de-escalation, reports say. They worry about their energy facilities, and one senior Gulf official said some countries might object to strikes launched from bases on their soil. Hormuz matters because about a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through the strait, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

Number one is the diplomacy that may decide it. On Sunday, October twenty-fifth, according to the New York Times, Qatari mediators delivered a letter from Vice President JD Vance to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council. It proposed a meeting, with Vance leading the American side. President Trump described the outreach as being about medical supplies and denied directing it, while the Wall Street Journal had reported that he did. On Saturday, Rezaei said he had read the letter and not yet replied. He said the American tone had completely shifted. But he also said the Strait of Hormuz stays closed, and nuclear talks will not begin, until Washington meets Iran's seven conditions. Then today, Sunday, November first, Foreign Minister Araghchi said Iran and Qatar are discussing a plan to reopen the strait within two days. Qatar had proposed five. The catch is the conditions. By Araghchi's account, they include lifting sanctions, restoring oil waivers, releasing frozen funds, including money held in Qatar, and reducing American forces in the region. He called the Vance letter a positive step, but said no meetings with American officials are planned. The United States has not publicly answered the two-day plan, and every detail of it comes from Iranian officials. One Israeli channel, N12, reported a third American message that Rezaei called much better. No other outlet confirmed it. The New York Times reported that officials said direct talks could start as soon as next week, in Qatar or Turkey.

So what comes next? Start with the dates. November third: Americans vote in the midterms, and President Trump has said there will be no strikes before it. November fourth: a date named by one outlet for possible strikes. Iran's reply to the Vance letter is still pending, and both Rezaei and Araghchi say Washington must meet Iran's conditions first. In Israel, President Herzog's consultations start the clock on coalition talks. In Serbia, the new parliament has yet to name a government. Reports point two ways at once: preparations for strikes in the Gulf, and letters passing through Qatar. Which one wins, neither Washington nor Tehran has said. Not known yet: whether Washington will answer the two-day plan, and what Iran's reply to the Vance letter will say. Will the Strait of Hormuz reopen before December? Tell us in the comments: yes or no.
Iran wants sanctions lifted, oil waivers restored and frozen funds released. What do those words actually mean, and who pays for them? That is the question next Wednesday.

upload.description:
Five stories shaped the week of October 25 to November 1, 2026: Serbia's student movement winning a majority in preliminary results, Israel's election with no bloc at 61 seats, what Chancellor Merz is reported to say the Iran war has cost Europe in energy, reports that the US told Gulf states to prepare for possible strikes after the midterms, and the plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days that Iran's foreign minister says is under discussion, if Iran's conditions are met.
